newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian minister says sex case probe unhindered.
newsitem.headline: Belgian minister says sex case probe unhindered.

text.p: Belgium's justice minister has pledged to an angry public that a high court ruling to remove the popular magistrate leading a child sex and murder investigation would not hinder efforts to solve the case.
Monday's ruling has dealt another blow to a nation shaken as much by revelations of bungling by previous investigators and police on the case as by the horrors of the crimes so far uncovered.

"The work is going to continue, to get to the bottom of the investigation," Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck told Belgian television. "I will even consider if it is possible to designate a second investigating magistrate to reinforce the team."

Belgium's top court, the Cour de Cassation, ruled in favour of removing Jean-Marc Connerotte from the case because he had a free dish of pasta from a group helping parents of missing children, adding that a magistrate must remain impartial.
Outside the court in Brussels news of the ruling was greeted by howls of derision from around 700 protesters.

"I am disgusted. I don't want to be Belgian anymore," one demonstrator told Belgian television. "There are tears in my eyes. I am ashamed," said another. In the port city of Antwerp 300 more staged a demonstration of support.

Virtually no one in the country had wanted Connerotte removed from the case, including the country's top prosecutor Eliane Liekendael, who reluctantly sought his removal because he had breached the letter of the law.
The decision seems certain to fuel conspiracy theories among Belgians of a cover-up attempt by people in high places touched by the paedophile scandal.

Belgian radio quoted a statement from Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene calling on the population to respect the court's decision which it said was made according with the law and the separation of political and judicial powers.

Police have so far uncovered the bodies of four missing girls and rescued two others who had been sexually abused. Thirteen people, including chief suspect and convicted rapist Marc Dutroux, have been arrested over the affair.
An emotional Paul Marchal, whose daughter An's body was found in the garden of a house owned by Dutroux, said after the ruling: "It is the beginning of the end...justice is dead."

Under Belgium's criminal law system, the investigating magistrate must be an impartial detective, building up a case file both for and against prosecution. The public prosecutor then decides whether the case should go to trial.

Lawyers for Dutroux and businessman Michel Nihoul argued Connerotte had shown bias by attending a dinner arranged by a parental support group, at which the two rescued victims of Dutroux were also present.
"For 14 months they let Dutroux and Nihoul run free. This decision is like spitting on the tombs of Julie and Melissa," Gino Russo, the father of Melissa, told reporters.
Eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo disappeared in June 1995. Their bodies were found two months ago entombed on a property owned by Dutroux. They had starved to death.
Parents of dead and missing children did welcome the ruling that responsibility for the investigation will stay in the southern town of Neufchateau under regional public prosecutor Michel Bourlet.
Connerotte and Bourlet are widely seen as the only honest investigators capable of bringing the affair to a conclusion.

"The fact that it remains in Neufchateau is a very important element because it means Bourlet will remain in charge," Laurent Arnauts, the lawyer for the parents of Loubna Benaissa, missing since 1992, told Reuters after the ruling.
"We think it is a good compromise between the rights of the defence and the need to keep people's confidence in the system," he added.
